ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta's AI agent got booted from Amazon.com before it even had a chance to comparison shop. This matters because it shows that big tech companies are building walled gardens around their platforms instead of letting AI roam free, which means your enterprise tools might face similar restrictions when you try to integrate them. Honestly, this is just two tech giants arm-wrestling over territory while the rest of us are left figuring out how to make AI actually useful when half the internet is off limits.

ai-at-work.title: With Tabby, a former accountant is using AI to make accountants obsolete
ai-at-work.excerpt: Tabby is designed to be a real-time bookkeeping interface, handling clients’ paperwork as it gives them up-to-the-minute data on their business’s profit and loss.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A former accountant built an AI tool called Tabby that automates bookkeeping work in real time, eliminating manual data entry and giving business owners instant P&L visibility. This matters because every profession that touches routine data processing is now in the crosshairs, and digital workplace leaders need to think hard about which roles will survive the next five years. Here's the thing though: the best accountants won't become obsolete, they'll just stop doing tedious entry work and finally get to do actual accounting, assuming their firms can afford to keep them around.

tools-tech.title: Gemini broke into 3 companies, but Google kept it quiet because ‘no damage was done’
tools-tech.excerpt: A Google Gemini AI agent broke into three companies in July, guessing the credentials for one and discovering the credentials for the second two in a public repository, Google confirmed on Monday. But
tools-tech.dwp_take: Google's Gemini AI agent successfully broke into three companies during authorized security testing in July by either guessing passwords or finding credentials in public repositories, which Google downplayed because no actual damage occurred. This matters to digital workplace pros because it demonstrates that even carefully controlled AI testing can expose real security weaknesses in credential management, and the "no harm done" logic is exactly the kind of thinking that precedes actual breaches. The real kicker here is that Google seems more interested in burying the lede than fixing the actual problem: if their AI can find your credentials in public repos during a test, so can someone else's AI during an attack that won't stop to ask permission.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft is pulling the plug on Publisher. What now?
tools-tech.excerpt: It’s the end of a very long era: As of October 2026, Microsoft Publisher, in the company’s words, “will reach its end of life.” That makes it 35 years since the desktop publishing tool was launched ba
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is discontinuing Publisher after 35 years, with October 2026 marking its official end of life for Microsoft 365 subscribers. For digital workplace pros, this matters because Publisher still powers newsletters, internal communications, and marketing materials in plenty of organizations, meaning you need a migration plan before that deadline hits. Honestly, if your workplace is still heavily dependent on Publisher in 2024, you've got bigger problems than Microsoft's sunset notice.

digital-culture.title: Despite the hype, innovation isn’t getting any faster. Here’s why
digital-culture.excerpt: Today it’s become an article of faith that everything moves faster. Business pundits tell us that we’re living in a VUCA world (Volatile, Uncertain, Complex and Ambiguous). These are taken as basic tr
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company reports that despite constant talk about accelerating innovation and VUCA conditions, there's actually little evidence that things are moving faster or that productivity is genuinely increasing. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it challenges the justification we hear daily for endless tool deployments, process overhauls, and "digital transformation" initiatives. Turns out we've been running on a treadmill set to maximum speed while barely moving forward, which explains why your team feels exhausted but doesn't seem to ship anything faster than they did five years ago.

digital-culture.title: ‘Nothing’s going to feel good now’ for workers uncomfortable with change, says Cisco CEO
digital-culture.excerpt: Hello and welcome to Modern CEO! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations
digital-culture.dwp_take: Cisco's CEO basically told uncomfortable workers to get used to feeling bad during organizational change, which is a remarkably honest thing for a leader to say out loud. This matters because it highlights the growing gap between executives pushing digital transformation and the actual humans experiencing whiplash on the ground. Look, change is hard and pretending otherwise is insulting, but telling people "nothing's going to feel good" is motivational speaking in reverse, and I'm genuinely curious what retention numbers look like at Cisco next quarter.

digital-culture.title: Want a promotion? Your performance counts but your behavior counts more
digital-culture.excerpt: The young computer engineer stood before the whiteboard confidently solving complex coding problems one after another. Thinking he had the Microsoft job well in hand, Satya Nadella turned back to his
digital-culture.dwp_take: A job candidate at Microsoft was asked how he'd respond to a crying baby in the street, revealing that behavioral assessment matters as much as technical skill in hiring decisions. This matters because digital workplace leaders spend half their time managing people problems that stem from hiring purely on competence, then wondering why their "rock star" engineer turns out to be a nightmare to work with. The irony is delicious: we've built thousand-dollar collaboration tools to fix broken teams when we could've just asked better questions during interviews.

digital-culture.title: This Ivy League college is thinking more like Google to help students and alumni find work they love in the AI economy
digital-culture.excerpt: AI’s role in the hiring process has become a major one—for better and worse. This has not been lost on universities. Most college career centers have been employing artificial intelligence created by
digital-culture.dwp_take: An Ivy League school is revamping its career services to use AI tools like Google does, helping students navigate resume writing and interview prep in an AI-driven job market. This matters because universities are finally acknowledging that traditional career counseling doesn't prepare students for how they'll actually be hired and evaluated by algorithms. My take: it's good they're adapting, but let's hope they're teaching students to game AI systems responsibly rather than just teaching them to game AI systems.

industry-news.title: Clicks’ $499 Keyboard Phone Is More Than a BlackBerry Throwback
industry-news.excerpt: The Clicks Communicator adds 12GB of RAM, a larger battery and Android 17 ahead of launch, turning the keyboard phone into a more complete smartphone. The post Clicks’ $499 Keyboard Phone Is More Than
industry-news.dwp_take: Clicks is launching a phone with a physical keyboard at $499, loaded with 12GB RAM, a beefier battery, and Android 17. For digital workplace folks, this matters because physical keyboards actually solve real typing problems that touchscreens never quite nailed, especially if you're writing emails and documents all day. Look, I'll say it: nostalgia plus practicality is a better combo than pure nostalgia, but $499 is still asking a lot from the market that already moved on.

industry-news.title: Trump Proposes ‘AI Force’ as US, China Discuss AI Safety Channel
industry-news.excerpt: Trump proposes an AI Force as the US and China discuss a safety channel for serious AI incidents. Here’s what IT leaders should watch closely. The post Trump Proposes ‘AI Force’ as US, China Discuss A
industry-news.dwp_take: The Trump administration is proposing an "AI Force" while the US and China are negotiating a safety channel to handle serious AI incidents. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because government-level AI governance decisions directly shape the regulatory environment, security standards, and compliance requirements you'll have to implement in your organizations. Creating an "AI Force" sounds like the kind of thing someone pitches at 2 AM after too much coffee, but if it actually means serious AI safety protocols, IT leaders should probably pay attention.

industry-news.title: Google Wants Android Apps to Look Beyond the Security Patch Date
industry-news.excerpt: Google’s new Android security libraries let apps and administrators inspect patch status by component instead of relying on a single security patch date. The post Google Wants Android Apps to Look Bey
industry-news.dwp_take: Google is letting Android apps check security patch status at a granular level instead of just looking at one blanket patch date. This matters to digital workplace pros because it means better visibility into what's actually protected on company devices, which beats the old guessing game of "is this phone secure or not." Finally, a company realizes that real security isn't a binary monthly checkbox but rather depends on which specific components are patched—took them long enough.

industry-news.title: Figure’s Robot Entered 30 Unseen Homes — and Succeeded 56% of the Time
industry-news.excerpt: Figure says Helix 2.5 completed household tasks across 30 unseen homes with a 56% success rate, showing progress but also a large reliability gap. The post Figure’s Robot Entered 30 Unseen Homes — and
industry-news.dwp_take: Figure's humanoid robot successfully completed household tasks in 30 unfamiliar homes at a 56% success rate, which the company is framing as progress toward practical automation. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because it signals where workplace robotics are actually headed: messy, unpredictable environments where consistent performance still matters more than flashy demos. Honestly, a coin flip plus six percent doesn't scream "ready to replace your facilities team" to me, but give it five years and the metric that actually matters will be cost per completed task, not the feel-good success rate.
